meta.blurb: In December 1831 a young Charles Darwin sailed from England on a small survey ship and did not come home for almost five years. Travel with him through jungle, ice, earthquake and volcanic islands, and watch a great idea begin.
meta.bible: Charles Darwin: English naturalist, born 12 February 1809, so 22 when the voyage began. Robert FitzRoy: the young captain of HMS Beagle, aged 26 at the start. John Henslow: Darwin's Cambridge teacher, who recommended him. The Beagle: a small British survey ship with about seventy people aboard; it left Devonport near Plymouth on 27 December 1831 and reached Falmouth on 2 October 1836. Its task was to chart coasts, especially in South America, and to measure the world's longitudes with many Chronometers. Darwin's book is the Journal of his travels, first published in 1839; later readers call it The Voyage of the Beagle. Places in order: Cape Verde Islands (the island of St Jago), Bahia and Rio de Janeiro in Brazil, Montevideo, Punta Alta, Patagonia, Port Desire, Santa Cruz, Tierra del Fuego, Woollya, the Beagle Channel, the Falkland Islands, Chiloé, Valparaíso, Valdivia, Concepción, Osorno, the Andes, Portillo, Uspallata, Lima, the Galápagos Islands, Tahiti, New Zealand, the Bay of Islands, Sydney, the Blue Mountains, the Keeling Islands, Mauritius, Cape Town, St Helena, Ascension, the Azores, Shrewsbury. People: Jemmy Button, York Minster and Fuegia Basket, three Fuegians who had been taken to England and were brought home; Richard Matthews, a missionary; Nicholas Lawson, the vice-governor of the Galápagos; Charles Lyell, author of Principles of Geology; John Gould, a bird expert; Richard Owen, an expert on fossils; John Herschel, an astronomer at Cape Town; Napoleon, whose tomb is on St Helena. Key terms: Naturalist, Specimens, Fossils, Megatherium, Glyptodon, Toxodon, Sloth, Armadillo, Gauchos, Lasso, Bolas, Rhea, Pampas, Guanacos, Warrah, Glacier, Earthquake, Volcano, Hammock, Iguanas, Tortoises, Mockingbirds, Finches, Platypus, Kangaroo, Coral, Atoll, Lagoon, Reef, Corroboree, Slavery, Fuegians, Maori, Tahitians, Aboriginal, Chronometers, Geology, Andes, Cordillera. Voice: warm, curious and plain, in the first person plural or third person; Darwin is young, keen, often seasick and always collecting. Dates and numbers are real or marked as about; nothing is invented.

B1B2: On 27 December 1831, a small ship called the Beagle finally left Devonport, after gales had held it in port. Among the crew was Charles Darwin, who was twenty-two years old and very excited.
Darwin was asked to go as a naturalist and as a companion for the young captain, Robert FitzRoy. His teacher, Professor Henslow, had suggested him, and his uncle persuaded his father to let him go.
About seventy people lived on the Beagle, which was small and crowded. Darwin slept in a hammock in a tiny room beside the chart table, and he had brought a new book about geology by Charles Lyell.
The first stop was St Jago, in the Cape Verde Islands. In a cliff of black volcanic rock, Darwin found a white band of shells far above the sea, so the land must have risen.

In Brazil, Darwin entered a tropical forest for the first time, and it filled him with wonder. There were enormous trees, brilliant flowers and butterflies, and he wrote that he could hardly describe what he felt.
Near Rio de Janeiro, Darwin spent weeks collecting insects, spiders and plants. He rode out on horseback with a guide, and he often came back with his boxes full of new things.
In Brazil, Darwin saw slavery with his own eyes, and he hated it. He argued sharply with Captain FitzRoy, who defended it, and for a short time it seemed that Darwin might have to leave the ship.
While the Beagle surveyed the coast, Darwin often travelled over land. He rode across the grassy plains with gauchos, the horsemen of South America, and he slept outdoors under the stars.
At a place called Punta Alta, Darwin found huge bones sticking out of the cliff. They belonged to enormous animals that no longer lived, including a giant sloth and a creature like a huge armadillo.
Darwin noticed something strange: the extinct giants were like the smaller animals that still live in South America. He began to wonder why the old and new animals of one place should be so alike.

The gauchos used ropes with heavy balls, called bolas, to catch animals. Darwin tried one himself, but the ropes wrapped around his own horse's legs, and the gauchos laughed until they could hardly stand.

At Christmas, the crew roasted a large bird called a rhea, and everyone enjoyed the dinner. Only when it was half eaten did Darwin realise it was a rarer, smaller kind that he had been hoping to find.
Patagonia, in the far south, is a wide and dry land of stones and low bushes. Darwin crossed it with a small party, and he found that these empty plains stayed in his mind for years.
The Beagle was also bringing three people home to Tierra del Fuego, at the very south of South America. They were Jemmy Button, York Minster and Fuegia Basket, who had spent time in England.
The Fuegians lived in a cold, wet land with very little clothing, and they kept small fires burning even in their canoes. Darwin was shocked at first by how different their lives were from his own.
At a bay called Woollya, the crew built huts and planted a small garden. The missionary Richard Matthews was to stay there, together with the three Fuegians who had come back from England.
In the Beagle Channel, great blue glaciers ran right down to the sea. A huge piece of ice once broke off and made a wave that nearly wrecked the boats, until the men pulled them up the beach.
In the Falkland Islands, Darwin met a wild fox that was not afraid of people. He wrote that it would probably disappear when people settled the islands, and sadly it did, in the late 1800s.
A year later, the Beagle came back to Woollya and found Jemmy Button. He was thin and wore only a blanket, and he looked sad, but he spoke some English and gave the crew gifts.
In 1834, Darwin fell ill at Valparaíso, in Chile, after a long trip into the mountains. He stayed in bed at a friend's house for about a month, and then he slowly got better.
The Beagle then sailed north along the coast of Chile. The island of Chiloé was rainy and covered with thick green forest, and Darwin found it a very beautiful place.
In January 1835, Darwin saw the volcano Osorno erupt in the night. Even from far away he could see a great red glow, and he learned that other volcanoes along the Andes had erupted too.
On 20 February 1835, Darwin was resting in a wood near Valdivia when a sudden earthquake shook the ground. It lasted about two minutes, and he found that he could hardly stand up.
When the Beagle reached Concepción, the town had been broken to pieces. Hardly a house was standing, and a huge sea wave had washed over the shore, so the damage was terrible to see.
Darwin and the captain noticed that the land near Concepción had risen by a few feet. Beds of mussels that had lived under the water now lay high and dry above the tide.
In March 1835, Darwin set out to cross the Andes, the huge mountain range between Chile and Argentina. He rode a mule with a guide, and the path climbed higher and higher through rock and snow.
Near the top of the pass, Darwin found fossil seashells in the rock, more than 3,500 metres above the sea. He knew at once that this high land must once have been under the ocean.
On the other side of the mountains, at Uspallata, Darwin found some trees turned to stone. They were still standing upright, and they showed that the land there had once been low, near the sea.

Darwin decided that the Andes had risen little by little, over a very long time, by many earthquakes and eruptions. This matched what Charles Lyell had written, and it helped Darwin to think in terms of deep time.
In July 1835 the Beagle reached the port of Callao, near Lima, in Peru. The sky was grey and foggy, and the land was dry, because it almost never rains there.

In September 1835, the Beagle arrived at the Galápagos Islands, far out in the Pacific. The islands were made of black lava, with dry bushes and cactus, and Darwin was going to spend five weeks there.
Darwin saw large dark lizards called marine iguanas, which swim in the sea and eat seaweed. He found them ugly, and he threw one into the water, but it kept coming back to him on the rocks.
Darwin met the giant tortoises, which were so big that he sat on one and rode it. The governor's deputy told him that each island has its own kind of tortoise, but Darwin did not pay much attention.

Darwin noticed that the mockingbirds on different islands were a little different from one another. In his notes, he wrote that if this was true, it would be worth studying the animals of these islands very carefully.
Darwin also collected many small finches, but he did not always mark which island each one came from. Only later did an expert tell him they were about a dozen kinds of finch, all closely related.
The animals of the Galápagos had never learned to fear people, so they were very tame. Darwin once pushed a hawk off a branch with the end of his gun, and it hardly seemed to mind.

In November 1835, the Beagle reached Tahiti, a beautiful green island in the Pacific. Darwin walked up a valley with two guides, and he wrote warmly about how friendly and cheerful the Tahitian people were.
In December 1835, the Beagle sailed into the Bay of Islands in New Zealand. Darwin visited a farm run by English missionaries, which had green hedges and fields, and he also met Maori people.

In January 1836, the Beagle arrived in Sydney, in Australia. Darwin was impressed by the young town, and he rode inland across the Blue Mountains, which were wild and full of strange plants and animals.

In the hills inland, Darwin saw a platypus swimming in a quiet pond. He wondered why Australian animals are so unlike those of other countries, and he wrote that a doubter might imagine two different makers.

One night near Bathurst, Darwin watched a group of Aboriginal people dance around a fire in a gathering called a corroboree. He admired their skill, and he wrote sadly that wherever Europeans settled, the local people suffered.
In April 1836, the Beagle reached the Keeling Islands in the Indian Ocean. They are a ring of low coral islands with palm trees around a calm lagoon, and Darwin had long wanted to see such a place.

Darwin worked out an idea about how these coral rings, called atolls, are made. A volcanic island slowly sinks, while coral keeps growing upward around its edge, until only a ring is left above the water.
After a stop in Mauritius, the Beagle reached Cape Town, in South Africa. There Darwin had the honour of meeting the famous astronomer Sir John Herschel, whose writing he had greatly admired.

At the island of St Helena, Darwin visited the tomb where the French emperor Napoleon had been buried. At Ascension Island, he received letters saying that scientists at home were already talking about his collections.
By now Darwin was tired of the sea and longed to be home. The Beagle first sailed back to Brazil and then to the Azores, and he wrote that he hated every wave that kept him from England.
On 2 October 1836, the Beagle finally reached Falmouth, in England. The voyage had lasted four years and nine months, and Darwin left the ship at once and hurried to his family's home in Shrewsbury.
Back in England, Darwin gave his huge collections to experts. Richard Owen studied the fossil bones, and John Gould studied the birds, and between them they told Darwin what he had really found.

In 1837, Darwin began private notebooks about how species might change over time. In one he drew a small branching tree and wrote the words I think above it, and in 1839 he published the Journal of his voyage.

Darwin later said that the voyage was the most important event in his life, because it decided his whole career. Captain FitzRoy also became well known later, and he helped to start weather forecasting in Britain.
C1C2: On 27 December 1831, after a delay caused by wild gales, the little ship Beagle slipped out of Devonport and set her bow towards the open Atlantic. Among the crew stood a twenty-two-year-old named Charles Darwin, who had never been to sea before and who would soon be wretchedly seasick. He could not have guessed that the journey ahead, which would last almost five years, was going to shape the whole of his life.

Darwin had been invited to come as a naturalist and as a gentleman companion for the captain, Robert FitzRoy, who was only twenty-six and often lonely in command. His teacher, Professor Henslow, had recommended him, and his father, who disliked the plan, finally gave way when a favourite uncle took Darwin's side. It is said that FitzRoy almost refused him because of the shape of his nose, which he feared showed too little energy.

The Beagle was a small ship carrying about seventy people, and space was so scarce that Darwin slung his hammock in a cramped cabin beside the chart table. His shelves held a new book, Charles Lyell's Principles of Geology, which taught that the Earth had been shaped by slow, ordinary forces over immense spans of time. The captain's task was to chart difficult coasts and to measure the world with a collection of delicate clocks, while Darwin's was to look, to collect and to wonder.

The first landing was at St Jago, one of the Cape Verde Islands, where Darwin climbed among black volcanic rocks under a fierce sun. High in the cliff, running level for miles, he found a pale band of shells and coral that had once lain on the sea floor, and the meaning was inescapable: the land had risen. With Lyell's book in his mind, he saw for the first time that he could read the history of a place directly from its stones.

At Bahia, in Brazil, Darwin walked into a tropical forest for the first time, and he was almost overcome by delight. Enormous trees hung with climbing plants towered above him, brilliant butterflies flickered through the green gloom, and every sound and scent was new. He wrote that such a scene was hard to describe, and that the mind seemed unable to hold so many wonders at once.

Around Rio de Janeiro, Darwin gave himself up to collecting, filling his boxes with insects, spiders, plants and shells that no European had examined carefully. He made long journeys on horseback with a guide, sleeping in country houses, and he came to love the sight of the forest-covered hills rising above the bay. Every day brought some creature or flower that he could not put a name to, and he was happier than he had ever been.

In Brazil Darwin saw slavery at close quarters, and what he saw filled him with disgust and shame, for he came from a family that had long opposed it. When the captain defended a slave owner's claim that his slaves were content, the two men quarrelled so fiercely that Darwin thought he might have to leave the ship. FitzRoy apologised the next day, and their friendship, though often strained, survived the long years ahead.

While the crew of the Beagle spent months measuring coastlines, Darwin often left the ship to travel across the land, covering long distances on horseback. He rode with the gauchos, the skilled horsemen of the great grassy plains, slept beneath the stars with his saddle for a pillow and learned to cook meat over an open fire. It was a rough life, but it gave him a far better idea of the continent than any harbour could.

At Punta Alta, near the coast of Argentina, Darwin discovered a cliff in which enormous bones lay buried among sea shells. They belonged to giant animals that had vanished, including a great ground sloth and a creature armoured like a giant armadillo. He dug them out with great care, wrapped them in cloth and packed them on board to be sent home to England.

As he studied the bones, Darwin noticed something that puzzled him deeply: the extinct giants closely resembled the smaller sloths and armadillos still living in the same part of the world. If each kind of animal had been made separately, he asked himself, why should the dead and the living of one continent be so alike? It was only a question for now, but it would trouble him for years.

The gauchos hunted with the bolas, a set of weighted ropes that they flung so that the cords wound round an animal's legs, and they made it look effortless. Darwin tried one himself, but the balls struck his own horse and tangled its legs, and the gauchos were so amused that they could scarcely sit upright in their saddles. He took the joke well, and he wrote about it afterwards with good humour.

At Christmas the party roasted a large flightless bird, and everyone made a hearty dinner of it. Only when the meal was half eaten did Darwin realise that this was the rarer, smaller kind of rhea, a species he had been hoping to discover for science. He rescued the head, the neck, the legs and some of the feathers from the remains, and the bird was later named in his honour.

In the far south lay Patagonia, a vast and arid land of shingle and thorny scrub where guanacos grazed and the wind never seemed to rest. Darwin crossed it with a small party, and though there was little there that most travellers would call beautiful, he found that the emptiness stayed with him. Years later, he wrote, he could still see those wide dry plains more clearly than the green fields of home.

At the tip of South America, in the stormy land called Tierra del Fuego, the Beagle was carrying three passengers home. They were Jemmy Button, York Minster and Fuegia Basket, who had been taken to England two years earlier and had learned English and some English habits. Captain FitzRoy hoped that a missionary and a small settlement would help them, a plan that Darwin watched with growing doubt.

The people who lived here, the Fuegians, endured storms and freezing rain with little more than a skin across their shoulders, and they kept small fires burning even in their canoes. Darwin was shocked by how different their way of life was from his own, and he did not hide his first, unkind reaction in his journal. Yet he also saw that they were skilful and quick, and that their lives were hard because the land was hard.

At Woollya, the crew of the Beagle built three huts, dug a vegetable garden and unloaded a great pile of goods that FitzRoy had bought as gifts. The young missionary Richard Matthews was to live there with the three Fuegians who had returned from England, in the hope of teaching and helping the local people. Within a few days the neighbours had begun to take what they pleased, and the plan began to fall apart.

Along the Beagle Channel, vast glaciers of blue ice crept down from the mountains and ended in cliffs above the water, which Darwin thought the most beautiful sight in the region. When a great mass of ice broke away and crashed into the sea, the wave it raised rushed along the shore and nearly swept away the boats. The sailors, running forward, seized them just in time and dragged them to safety high up the beach.

On the Falkland Islands Darwin met a wild fox so tame that it hardly noticed men, and a sailor once killed one by leaving a piece of meat in one hand and a knife in the other. Darwin predicted that this unique animal, found nowhere else in the world, would be wiped out as soon as people settled the islands. His forecast was right, for the last of these foxes was killed in the 1870s.

When the Beagle returned to the Fuegian coast in 1834, a thin man in a scrap of blanket paddled out to meet her, and it took the sailors a moment to recognise Jemmy Button. His hair was long, he had lost his English manners, and Darwin was dismayed at the change in his appearance. Yet Jemmy dined with the officers, brought presents of furs and spearheads, and made it clear that he preferred his own life and had no wish to return to England.

In September 1834, after an exhausting journey in the hills, Darwin fell seriously ill at Valparaíso and lay in bed at a friend's house for about a month. The ship waited in the bay, his books and notes stacked beside him, and he grew impatient with his own weakness while the weeks went by. By October he had recovered well enough to rejoin the Beagle, and he went on with his work as eagerly as ever.

From the cold south the Beagle sailed north into the waters of Chile, where the island of Chiloé lay under a thick blanket of rain and forest. Small villages stood along the shore, the people grew potatoes and kept pigs, and the green of the trees came right down to the water. Darwin explored by boat and on foot, and he noted the plants and the wildlife with his usual care.

In January 1835, from the shore of Chiloé, Darwin watched the volcano Osorno burst into fire in the darkness, a great red glow shining on the clouds above its summit. He later learned that two other volcanoes in the Andes had erupted at about the same time, which suggested that they were somehow connected deep underground. The sight impressed on him, more than any book could, how restless the Earth's crust really is.

On 20 February 1835, Darwin was lying down to rest in a wood near Valdivia when the ground began to shudder beneath him. The earthquake lasted about two minutes, and he found it surprisingly hard to keep his balance, as though the solid earth had suddenly turned to liquid. Nothing in his reading about geology had quite prepared him for the sensation, which he described as lasting in the memory.

When the Beagle reached the port of Concepción, soon afterwards, she found the city reduced to heaps of broken walls and fallen roofs. A great wave from the sea had swept in after the shock, scattering boats and timber over the shore, and the survivors were camping in the open. Darwin wrote that it was the most awful and interesting spectacle he had ever seen, and he did not mean it lightly.

Examining the coast, Darwin and FitzRoy found proof that the earthquake had lifted the land by a few feet, for beds of mussels that once lived under the water now lay bare above the high tide mark. This was exactly the kind of slow, repeated change that Lyell had described, and here it was happening before their eyes. If a single earthquake could raise the shore by so much, he reasoned, then many earthquakes over a very long time could raise a mountain range.

In March 1835, Darwin left the coast of Chile to cross the Andes, the immense mountain range that separates Chile from Argentina. With a guide and a train of mules he climbed by narrow tracks through the Portillo Pass, over loose rock and past banks of snow, breathing hard in the thin air. It was the most arduous journey he had yet attempted, and he enjoyed every mile of it.

Near the summit of the pass, set in the bare rock far above the clouds, Darwin found fossil sea shells, more than 3,500 metres above sea level. This was evidence he could hold in his hand, since the bed on which he stood must once have lain on the floor of an ocean. He felt that he had come across something enormous, though he did not yet know quite how to say it.

On the far side of the range, at Uspallata, Darwin came upon a group of trees that had been turned into stone, still standing where they had grown. They had evidently flourished on a low shore, been sunk beneath the sea, buried in layers of lava and sand, and then raised again to a great height. It was a story of slow, repeated lifting and sinking that would have taken a vast span of time.

Sitting among the peaks, Darwin concluded that the Andes had been built up gradually, through countless earthquakes and eruptions, over a span of time too great to imagine. This was exactly the picture Lyell had drawn, and Darwin had now seen it with his own eyes on a grand scale. His mind was opening to the idea that great changes may be the sum of small ones, a lesson he would later apply to living things.

In July 1835, the Beagle anchored at Callao, the port of Lima, under a blanket of grey fog that seemed to hang over the coast of Peru throughout the year. Rain almost never falls there, yet the air is damp and the sky is dull, and Darwin found the whole place drab and unpleasant. He was glad that it was only a stop on the way, for the best was still ahead.

In September 1835 the Beagle came to the Galápagos Islands, a scattering of volcanic islands lying in the Pacific Ocean about a thousand kilometres off the coast of Ecuador. The shores were black with lava, the bushes grey and stunted, and the whole landscape looked burnt and sterile at first sight. Darwin would spend about five weeks there, and the creatures he found among those barren rocks would trouble and inspire him for the rest of his life.

On the black rocks lay hundreds of large dark lizards, the marine iguanas, which swim out into the sea to feed on seaweed and then return to bask in the sun. Darwin thought them hideous creatures, and he threw one far into the waves several times to see what it would do, but it always swam straight back to the same spot. He decided that its instinct told it the water was dangerous, and the land was its only refuge.

Darwin discovered the giant tortoises, enormous creatures that plodded slowly through the highlands, and he amused himself by sitting on the back of one and riding it. The vice-governor of the islands, a man named Nicholas Lawson, told him that he could tell at a glance which island a tortoise had come from, but Darwin did not take the remark seriously. It was one of the greatest clues of the whole voyage, and for the moment he let it slip past.

Darwin noticed that the mockingbirds on different islands seemed to differ a little from one another, and he wrote down in his notes that, if this proved true, the animals of the islands would be well worth close study. It was only a passing remark, but it shows that the idea was already stirring in him, half-formed. A scientist who sees a puzzle and writes it down has already done half of the work.

Darwin shot and kept many small finches, which looked so alike that he did not trouble to note carefully which island each had come from. Back in England, the bird expert John Gould examined them and announced that they belonged to about a dozen separate but closely related species, each with a beak suited to its own food. Darwin then had to piece together their origins from the labelled collections of his shipmates, and the finches became famous.

The creatures of the Galápagos had lived for ages without meeting any human enemies, and Darwin found them astonishingly tame. He pushed a hawk off a branch with the muzzle of his gun, a small bird sipped water from a jug in his hand, and the doves hardly moved as he walked by. Fear of man, he realised, is not something that animals are born with, but a lesson that has to be learned over generations.

In November 1835 the Beagle arrived at Tahiti, a lush island ringed with coral and crowned by jagged green mountains. Darwin spent two days walking up a deep valley with two local guides, who cooked fish for him over a fire and carried his bundle, and he wrote warmly of their cheerfulness and good manners. He found the people far more agreeable than he had expected, and much of what he had read about them in books proved to be out of date.

In December 1835 the Beagle sailed into the Bay of Islands, in New Zealand, where English missionaries and Maori communities lived side by side. Darwin walked inland to a mission farm whose fields, hedges and flowers looked remarkably like home, and he also met Maori men, whose tattooed faces made a strong impression on him. He stayed only a short time, and he left with the feeling that he had seen a country in the middle of great change.

In January 1836, the Beagle arrived at Sydney, where Darwin was impressed by the busy young town and by the energy of its settlers. He hired a guide and rode inland across the Blue Mountains, through woods of strange grey-green trees, where there were kangaroos and many unfamiliar birds. For a naturalist who had spent years in South America, it was like entering another planet.

Beside a quiet pond Darwin watched a platypus, a furry animal with a bill like a duck's, swimming and diving among the reeds. The animals of Australia struck him as so unlike those of other lands with similar climates that he wrote, half in jest, that a doubter might imagine two different makers had been at work. The question of why places differ as they do was still unanswered, but he was now asking it all the time.

One evening near Bathurst, Darwin watched a large gathering of Aboriginal men dance by firelight in a ceremony called a corroboree, and he admired the energy and rhythm of the performance. He also wrote, with evident sorrow, that wherever Europeans settled, death seemed to follow the original inhabitants, whose numbers were already falling. It is one of the more sobering passages in a book that is mostly cheerful.

In April 1836, the Beagle reached the Keeling Islands, a low ring of coral and coconut palms that encircles a calm, shallow lagoon in the Indian Ocean. Darwin had been thinking about such islands for months, and here at last he could examine one at close quarters, wading on the reef while the surf broke white beyond it. He found hermit crabs, land crabs that could crack a coconut and a sea so clear that every coral shone.

At the Keeling Islands Darwin tested an idea he had been forming, about how coral rings, known as atolls, come into being. A volcanic island, he proposed, slowly sinks beneath the sea while the coral growing around its edge builds steadily upward, until all that remains above the surface is a circle around a lagoon. Later studies, including deep drilling, largely supported the idea, which is still taught today.

After a brief stay at Mauritius, the Beagle rounded the southern tip of Africa and anchored at Cape Town, beneath the flat summit of Table Mountain. There, Darwin had the honour of meeting Sir John Herschel, the famous astronomer, whose books on scientific method he had studied closely since his student days. Visiting that great man in his garden was, for a young naturalist, a moment he would remember always.

On the remote island of St Helena, Darwin walked to the tomb of the French emperor Napoleon, who had died there in exile, and found it a simple grave under a willow tree. At Ascension, a few days later, he received letters from home which told him, to his astonishment, that his professor Henslow had read his specimens' descriptions to learned societies, and that his name was already known. The news made him impatient to arrive, and perhaps just a little proud of what he had done.

By now Darwin was weary of the sea, and his letters were full of longing for the fields and faces of home. The Beagle turned back to Bahia in Brazil to check her measurements, and then sailed north to the Azores, and every extra mile seemed to him an injury. He wrote that he hated the ocean and every wave in it, which was a remarkable thing for a man who had spent nearly five years on it.

On 2 October 1836, the Beagle dropped anchor at Falmouth, in the south-west of England, after a voyage of four years and nine months that had carried her all the way around the world. Darwin said a rapid farewell to the ship, took the first coach north and reached his family's home in Shrewsbury late at night, where his sisters and his father were asleep. It is said that his father, seeing him the next morning, remarked that the shape of his head had altered.

Back in England, Darwin handed his crates of specimens to the leading experts of the day. Richard Owen examined the fossil bones from South America and identified the giant sloth and its relatives, while John Gould studied the birds and showed that the Galápagos finches and mockingbirds were distinct species. Their verdicts gave Darwin's half-formed suspicions about change in nature a solid foundation of facts.

In 1837, Darwin began a series of private notebooks on how species might change, and in one of them he sketched a small branching tree with the words I think written above it. In 1839 he published the journal of his travels, a lively and observant account that quickly became popular with ordinary readers and made him widely known. It has never gone out of print, and later editions are often called The Voyage of the Beagle.

Looking back in old age, Darwin judged the voyage of the Beagle to have been by far the most important event of his life, since it set the whole course of his career. The ship had taught him to look, to collect, to question and to think in terms of vast spans of time, and from those habits came his later books. FitzRoy, too, found a new calling, for as head of an early weather office he is credited with the word forecast and with warnings that saved many sailors.
